Actions on Objectives

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Better-Auth SCIM global user deletion via /scim/v2/Users from unsanctioned caller · [LLM] Better-Auth SCIM profile/email rewrite fan-out across many /scim/v2/Users resources · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Better-Auth SCIM global user deletion via /scim/v2/Users from unsanctioned caller AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts DELETE requests to the better-auth SCIM Users endpoint (/scim/v2/Users/:id) coming from a source IP that has never previously driven SCIM traffic. On affected @better-auth/scim (>=1.4.0-beta.27 <=1.6.21, 1.7.0-beta.0-9) a low-privileged authenticated user can mint a SCIM token with a colliding provider ID and DELETE the global Better Auth user plus sessions. Legitimate SCIM deprovisioning originates from the IdP's fixed egress; a delete from a fresh caller IP is the collision-abuse signal. Rationale: Uses the exact endpoint string from the advisory (DELETE /scim/v2/Users/:id — the highest-impact non-org deletion path) and the baseline anti-join on caller IP to separate colliding-token abuse from legitimate IdP deprovisioning, which always comes from a fixed egress. No endpoint/EDR telemetry exists for an inbound HTTP authz flaw, so only web-log platforms are populated. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/scim/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/scim
ATT&CKT1531 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IdP (Entra/Okta) deprovisioning from a newly rotated egress IP not seen in the 30d baseline
  • IdP failover to a secondary datacenter with a different public IP
  • Scheduled SCIM connector migrated to a new host/IP
  • Authorized penetration test or SCIM integration testing against the endpoint
  • Admin manually calling the SCIM API from a jump host during troubleshooting
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the DELETE events; identify the caller IP, csUserName, User-Agent and the /Users/:id targets; confirm the IP is NOT your sanctioned IdP egress and decode the SCIM bearer token's provider ID to see if it collides with an SSO/OIDC/OAuth/social provider namespace. 2) Contain: Revoke the offending SCIM token, disable SCIM token generation (canGenerateToken) for non-privileged users, block the source IP, and restore deleted users/sessions from backup. 3) Hunt: Audit scimProvider rows for providerId values matching other account providers, review PUT/PATCH activity on the same endpoint from the same caller, and upgrade to @better-auth/scim 1.6.22 or 1.7.0-beta.10.
// Baseline = IPs that legitimately drove SCIM in the prior 30d (your IdP egress)
let SanctionedScimCallers = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where csUriStem has "/scim/v2/Users"
    | summarize by cIP;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csUriStem has "/scim/v2/Users"
| where csMethod == "DELETE"
| where scStatus in (200, 204)            // successful global-user deletion
| join kind=leftanti SanctionedScimCallers on cIP   // delete from an IP never before seen issuing SCIM
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csUserName, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName, Computer, sPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Better-Auth SCIM profile/email rewrite fan-out across many /scim/v2/Users resources AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single caller issuing PUT/PATCH updates against many distinct better-auth SCIM Users resources (/scim/v2/Users/:id). On affected @better-auth/scim, a colliding-provider-ID token can resolve SSO/OIDC-provisioned users it never provisioned and rewrite global profile fields; SCIM PUT/PATCH also changed email without the create-path uniqueness check and left emailVerified stale — enabling account takeover. A colliding token enumerating and rewriting >5 distinct user resources is the fan-out signal. Rationale: Targets the advisory's second write path — PUT/PATCH to /scim/v2/Users rewriting global email/profile fields via a colliding provider ID. dcount over distinct /Users/:id paths captures the enumerate-and-rewrite fan-out that separates one caller mutating many unowned users from a normal single-target IdP update. Threshold-based, so no Sigma emitted. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/scim/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/scim
ATT&CKT1098 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IdP bulk attribute sync (job title/department/manager) touching many users after an HR data change
  • Initial SCIM provisioning backfill writing all existing users at onboarding
  • IdP re-sync following a SCIM connector configuration change or schema update
  • IdP retry storm re-issuing PUT/PATCH after a transient failure
  • Scheduled reconciliation job that periodically re-pushes all mapped attributes
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the caller IP/csUserName and enumerate which /Users/:id resources were modified; decode the SCIM token provider ID and check whether it collides with an SSO/OIDC/OAuth/social provider namespace the caller does not own. 2) Contain: Revoke the SCIM token, restrict canGenerateToken, and for any user whose email was reassigned force emailVerified reset + password/session reset to block takeover of email-keyed login. 3) Hunt: Correlate with DELETE activity on the same endpoint, audit scimProvider rows for colliding providerId, verify no duplicate/hijacked email addresses were created, and upgrade to 1.6.22 / 1.7.0-beta.10.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "/scim/v2/Users"
| where csMethod in ("PUT", "PATCH")
| where scStatus between (200 .. 299)
| summarize WriteCount = count(),
            DistinctUserResources = dcount(csUriStem),
            Methods = make_set(csMethod),
            UserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by cIP, csUserName, sSiteName
| where DistinctUserResources > 5     // one caller rewriting >5 distinct /Users/:id resources = collision fan-out
| order by WriteCount desc

BlueNoroff ClickFix Defender tamper: exclude C:\Users + disable realtime monitoring AIInstallation High
Hunts the BlueNoroff Windows loader step that adds the entire C:\Users tree to Microsoft Defender's exclusion path and disables real-time monitoring before force-restarting Defender. Excluding all of C:\Users is a near-unique fingerprint of this stealer loader — legitimate admins almost never exclude the whole user tree. Rationale: Uses the article's exact loader behaviour — Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "C:\Users" plus Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring — which is corroborated verbatim by Arctic Wolf and GBHackers. Whole-user-tree exclusion is a rare, high-fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/bluenoroff-uses-clickfix-fileless-powershell-ai-generated-fake-zoom-meetings-to-target-web3-sector/ • https://gbhackers.com/bluenoroff-fake-meeting-kit/
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EDR/AV migration scripts temporarily adding path exclusions during product swap
  • Legacy backup or dev tooling that excludes a single user profile subfolder (rarely the whole C:\Users)
  • MDM/GPO baseline scripts toggling DisableRealtimeMonitoring in test rings
  • Security product installer stubs that disable Defender before install
  • Malware sandbox/analysis VMs pre-disabling Defender
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("services.exe","svchost.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full PowerShell command line and its parent chain — a BlueNoroff hit will show explorer.exe→powershell (ClickFix paste) and both an ExclusionPath C:\Users and a Defender restart. Confirm the user isn't IT/security. 2) Contain: isolate the host, re-enable Defender real-time protection, remove the C:\Users exclusion, and force a full scan; reset the user's Telegram session and browser credentials. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a downloaded/executed .vbs, wscript.exe reading browser profile dirs, and outbound to us.zoom.06webin.us / callsdk.online / weekly-up.online.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath" and ProcessCommandLine has @"C:\Users")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference","Set-MpPreference"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where (CommandLine has "ExclusionPath" and CommandLine has @"C:\Users")
     or (CommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring" and CommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference","Set-MpPreference"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BlueNoroff ClickFix Defender Exclusion of C\Users and Realtime Monitoring Disable
id: 6f2a9c14-3b81-4d5e-9a17-2c8e1f0b7d42
description: Detects PowerShell adding C:\Users to Defender exclusions or disabling real-time monitoring, matching the BlueNoroff Windows ClickFix loader
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/bluenoroff-zoom-phishing-kit-profiles.html
  - https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/bluenoroff-uses-clickfix-fileless-powershell-ai-generated-fake-zoom-meetings-to-target-web3-sector/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1562.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_exclude:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'ExclusionPath'
      - 'C:\Users'
  selection_disable:
    CommandLine|contains: 'DisableRealtimeMonitoring'
  condition: selection_img and (selection_exclude or selection_disable)
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe) ((@CommandLine:*ExclusionPath* AND @CommandLine:*Users*) OR @CommandLine:*DisableRealtimeMonitoring*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(ExclusionPath.{0,40}C:\\\\Users|DisableRealtimeMonitoring)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND ((Processes.process="*ExclusionPath*" AND Processes.process="*C:\\Users*") OR Processes.process="*DisableRealtimeMonitoring*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND ((Processes.process="*ExclusionPath*" AND Processes.process="*C:\\Users*") OR Processes.process="*DisableRealtimeMonitoring*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
BlueNoroff typosquatted Zoom/Teams infrastructure network contact AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network contact with the confirmed BlueNoroff phishing-kit and payload domains impersonating Zoom/Teams (06webin.us, 05ukweb.uk) and staging hosts (weekly-up.online, callsdk.online). These serve the fake meeting page, wallet fingerprinting and the 'Zoom SDK Update' ClickFix payload. Rationale: Domains us.zoom.06webin.us, zoom.05ukweb.uk, weekly-up.online and callsdk.online are the article's pre-extracted IOCs; matching on the registrable suffix also captures the actor's sub-domain-heavy typosquat scheme (us.zoom.06webin.us). Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/bluenoroff-fake-meeting-kit/ • https://crypto.news/north-korea-hackers-scan-crypto-wallets-through-fake-zoom-calls/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment or sandbox tooling actively resolving these IOC domains
  • Security researcher manually browsing the phishing page in a lab
  • Web proxy/URL-filtering appliance pre-fetching the domain for categorisation
  • A user who typo'd a real Zoom link and hit the squat once (still worth review)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that made the connection — a browser resolving 06webin.us/05ukweb.uk means the victim reached the fake meeting page; curl/powershell resolving callsdk.online/weekly-up.online means payload staging. 2) Contain: block all four domains at proxy/DNS, isolate the host if a non-browser process contacted them, and reset the user's Telegram + wallet credentials. 3) Hunt: check the host for the Defender-exclusion PowerShell, a dropped .vbs, wscript browser-profile reads, and (macOS) curl to api.telegram.org.

| order by Timestamp desc

ClickFix PowerShell loader spawning wscript to run downloaded VBScript AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the BlueNoroff Windows execution stage where the pasted ClickFix PowerShell command downloads a VBScript and launches it via wscript/cscript. Pivots on the powershell.exe → wscript.exe parent/child edge with a .vbs on the child command line — the file-based bridge unique to this loader. Rationale: The article states the ClickFix PowerShell loader 'downloads and executes a VBScript' — the powershell→wscript(.vbs) edge is the concrete process-tree signature of that bridge and is rare in benign estates. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/bluenoroff-uses-clickfix-fileless-powershell-ai-generated-fake-zoom-meetings-to-target-web3-sector/ • https://gbhackers.com/bluenoroff-fake-meeting-kit/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise deployment scripts where PowerShell invokes a signed .vbs installer helper
  • IT automation/login scripts chaining PowerShell into wscript
  • Vendor software update routines using VBScript wrappers
  • RMM tooling launching .vbs jobs from PowerShell
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","gpscript.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read both command lines — the parent PowerShell should show a download cradle (IWR/Net.WebClient) fetching the .vbs, and the parent chain likely traces to explorer.exe (ClickFix paste). Confirm the .vbs path (often %TEMP%/%APPDATA%). 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the wscript process, capture and hash the .vbs, and reset the user's Telegram/browser credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot to the Defender C:\Users exclusion, wscript reads of Chrome/Edge/Brave/Firefox profile dirs, and outbound to the four typosquat domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".vbs"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has ".vbs"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PowerShell Spawning WScript With VBScript (BlueNoroff ClickFix Loader)
id: c4a8f0d9-2e17-4b63-9f21-5a6d3c8b1e70
description: Detects powershell.exe launching wscript/cscript with a .vbs argument, matching the BlueNoroff ClickFix PowerShell-to-VBScript loader bridge
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/bluenoroff-zoom-phishing-kit-profiles.html
  - https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/bluenoroff-uses-clickfix-fileless-powershell-ai-generated-fake-zoom-meetings-to-target-web3-sector/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:

  - attack.t1059.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '.vbs'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe) @CommandLine:*.vbs*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\.vbs/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") AND Processes.process="*.vbs*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") AND Processes.process="*.vbs*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
WScript enumerating browser profiles for Telegram session and wallet extensions AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the BlueNoroff VBScript implant reading Chrome/Edge/Brave/Firefox/Opera/Vivaldi profile directories to locate Telegram Web session files and inventory installed wallet extensions (e.g. MetaMask). wscript/cscript touching browser User Data trees is anomalous and directly maps to the kit's wallet-reconnaissance and session-theft step. Rationale: Maps the article's VBScript implant that 'checks for Telegram Web-related files within Chrome, Edge, Brave, Firefox' and 'enumerates installed extensions ... matched against wallet extensions like MetaMask'. wscript reading browser User Data is intrinsically suspicious. Datadog left blank — file-read telemetry isn't captured by Sysmon EID 11. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/bluenoroff-fake-meeting-kit/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/bluenoroff-uses-clickfix-fileless-powershell-ai-generated-fake-zoom-meetings-to-target-web3-sector/
ATT&CKT1539 T1217
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browser profile backup/migration scripts implemented in VBScript
  • Enterprise DLP/inventory agents scanning browser dirs (usually not via wscript)
  • Bookmark/password-import helpers packaged as .vbs by IT
  • Antivirus quarantine of files inside a browser profile path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "backup"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the wscript instance is the BlueNoroff .vbs (check its parent PowerShell and the .vbs path) and list which browser artifacts it touched — Local State, Login Data, Local Extension Settings, Firefox profiles. 2) Contain: isolate host, revoke and re-issue the user's Telegram session (log out all devices), rotate any wallet/exchange credentials, and force browser password resets. 3) Hunt: enumerate wallet extension IDs present (MetaMask etc.), check for next-stage payload download, and review Telegram account for messages sent to the victim's contacts (self-propagation).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles", @"\Opera Software", @"\Vivaldi\User Data", @"\Chromium\User Data")
| summarize FilesTouched = dcount(FolderPath), SamplePath = any(FolderPath), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles", @"\Opera Software", @"\Vivaldi\User Data", @"\Chromium\User Data")
| summarize FilesTouched = dcount(TargetFilePath), SamplePath = any(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc

macOS BlueNoroff stealer exfiltrating to Telegram bot (Aurora channel) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the BlueNoroff macOS stealer's exfiltration step: a shell/curl process posting stolen Chrome master keys and system metadata to the hard-coded Telegram bot API (api.telegram.org/bot.../sendDocument|sendMessage) tied to the 'Aurora' channel. Targets the bot-token exfil pattern rather than generic Telegram app traffic. Rationale: Article states the macOS stealer exfiltrates Chrome master keys from the iCloud Keychain to a Telegram channel 'Aurora' with the bot token/chat ID hard-coded in the binary. The api.telegram.org/bot.../sendDocument command-line pattern is the concrete exfil fingerprint. Sentinel left blank — macOS process command lines are not available in this tenant's Sentinel tables (no DeviceProcessEvents equivalent). Cross-checked against: • https://crypto.news/north-korea-hackers-scan-crypto-wallets-through-fake-zoom-calls/ • https://gbhackers.com/bluenoroff-fake-meeting-kit/
ATT&CKT1567 T1555.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/SRE scripts that legitimately post alerts to a Telegram bot via curl
  • CI/CD or monitoring jobs using sendMessage for notifications
  • Personal Telegram-bot automation on a corporate Mac
  • Security tooling that itself notifies a Telegram channel
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/Downloads/", "/Volumes/", "/private/tmp/") or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code","node","python3")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the bot token and chat ID from the command line and check whether the parent process is a recently downloaded fake Zoom/Teams installer; sendDocument (file upload) is far more suspicious than sendMessage. 2) Contain: isolate the Mac, rotate Keychain-stored browser/wallet credentials and iCloud session, and (if authorised) report the bot token to Telegram for takedown. 3) Hunt: pull the installer binary for analysis, look for the initiating shell script download, and correlate the same host's earlier contact with the typosquat Zoom/Teams domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl","bash","sh","zsh","osascript")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "api.telegram.org/bot"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sendDocument","sendMessage")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl","bash","sh","zsh","osascript")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "api.telegram.org/bot"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sendDocument","sendMessage")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental

    category: process_creation

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

SecurityEvent

| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

Certighost Exploit Lets Low-Privileged Active Directory Users Impersonate a Domain Controller

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 17 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers H0j3n and Aniq Fakhrul published a working exploit on July 24 that lets a low-privileged Active Directory user obtain a certificate for a Domain Controller and authenticate as that machine. They codenamed the flaw Certighost. Because Domain Controller accounts carry directory replication rights, the resulting Kerberos credential can retrieve the krbtgt secret through DCSync.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AD CS CA server initiates SMB(445)+LDAP(389) to a non-DC host (Certighost chase relay) · [LLM] Domain Controller machine account obtains TGT via PKINIT certificate (Certighost impersonation) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Certighost Exploit Lets Low-Privileged Active Directory Users Impersonate a Doma
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Certighost precursor: domain computer account created by low-privileged user (MAQ abuse) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Directory replication / DCSync of secrets (krbtgt) via impersonated DC identity · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Certighost precursor: domain computer account created by low-privileged user (MAQ abuse) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the first step of the Certighost (CVE-2026-54121) chain where a normal Domain User creates a machine account under the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota (10) to supply the valid domain identity the CA needs. Flags Security event 4741 where the creator is an interactive user rather than a machine or provisioning account. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit precondition: a Domain Users account creating a computer account under the default MachineAccountQuota of 10. 4741 with a human creator (SubjectUserName not ending in $) is the cleanest DC-side telemetry for that step; corroborated by the researcher PoC's --computer-name behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.dataminr.com/resources/intel-brief/certighost-cve-2026-54121/ • https://www.it-connect.tech/certighost-cve-2026-54121-a-standard-ad-account-is-enough-to-impersonate-a-domain-controller/
ATT&CKT1136.002
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SCCM/MDT/Autopilot provisioning accounts pre-staging computer objects
  • Helpdesk staff joining new workstations to the domain
  • Delegated OU admins bulk-creating lab or VDI machine accounts
  • Backup/imaging service accounts re-creating rebuilt hosts
  • Legitimate delegated join accounts operating under MAQ
Suppression filter
| where Creator !in~ ("svc-sccm","svc-mdt","svc-domainjoin")   // populate with your approved provisioning accounts
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the creator (SubjectUserName) is an approved provisioning/join identity; note the new account name and creation time as pivot points. 2) Contain: if unexpected, disable the new computer object and the creating user, and check whether that machine account subsequently authenticated to the Enterprise CA. 3) Hunt: pivot on the new machine account and creator within a 2-hour window for CA-directed SMB(445)/LDAP(389) traffic (UC2), 4768 certificate logons (UC3), and directory replication (UC4) to confirm the full Certighost chain.
IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "Computer account created" or ActionType == "Account created"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where AccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
| project Timestamp, Creator = AccountName, CreatorDomain = AccountDomain, NewComputerAccount = TargetAccountUpn, DeviceName, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4741   // A computer account was created
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"   // exclude machine/DC-driven creation
| where SubjectUserName !in~ ("SYSTEM","ANONYMOUS LOGON")
| project TimeGenerated, DC = Computer, Creator = SubjectUserName, CreatorDomain = SubjectDomainName, NewComputerAccount = TargetUserName, TargetSid, Activity
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AD CS CA server initiates SMB(445)+LDAP(389) to a non-DC host (Certighost chase relay) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core Certighost trust-boundary failure: after receiving a request with attacker-supplied cdc/rmd attributes, the Enterprise CA connects out to the attacker's rogue LSA/SMB (445) and LDAP (389) listeners as if they were a Domain Controller. Surfaces any host that reaches a single remote endpoint on both 389 and 445 where that endpoint has never previously served LDAP (i.e. is not an established DC). Rationale: The article and the flow diagram both show the CA connecting out to the attacker's cdc host over SMB/LSA (445) and performing an LDAP chase (389). A remote host receiving both LDAP+SMB from a server while having no prior LDAP-serving history is a rogue-DC signature; the 30-day anti-join derives real DCs automatically so no asset list is hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgz6_WZR93lKBOoxTZvtu7b3fWT03SfhNZtwdqqWDAiolu_H_0WvZAPzpxFYGw_1dgmwDv8ox1oHDC0hiS3H0Wl_ggXkE96K-HbqD7Y39OGnkGnfWqs2GIEmMSlqRiNcZAiHfcri-WCM1PEjeTxY3_XkzgPSiG0FHQ3mac92JE0KgE1n140OwAFb_r93E0/s1700-e365/flow.png • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/public-exploit-enables-domain-controller-impersonation • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26
ATT&CKT1649 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A newly promoted Domain Controller (dcpromo) legitimately begins serving LDAP+SMB and has no 30-day history
  • New LDAP appliance / identity gateway (e.g. a directory sync host) coming online
  • IP re-use where a former non-DC address is reassigned to a DC
  • Vulnerability scanners probing 389 and 445 across the estate
  • Load-balancer VIPs fronting DC LDAP/SMB that rotate backends
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName has_any ("CA","PKI","CERT")   // optional: scope source to Enterprise CA hosts to cut new-DC-promo noise
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host is an Enterprise CA and the flagged RemoteIP/DstIpAddr is NOT a real Domain Controller (check DNS, ntdsutil/AD Sites, and whether it hosts CIFS/LDAP SPNs). 2) Contain: if the destination is not a DC, isolate it, block CA-to-that-host traffic, and stop CertSvc on the CA pending review; apply the KB (July 14 update) or set EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC off. 3) Hunt: correlate the CA's certificate issuance logs (4886/4887) around FirstSeen, then pivot on any DC$ certificate logon (UC3) and replication (UC4) from the same actor.
let lookback = 1d;
let KnownLdapServers = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where RemotePort == 389
    | summarize by RemoteIP;   // established LDAP servers approximate real DCs
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where RemotePort in (389, 445)
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| summarize Ports = make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), ConnCount = count(),
            InitProc = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName)
        by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| where set_has_element(Ports, 389) and set_has_element(Ports, 445)   // CA reached rogue host on LDAP + SMB
| join kind=leftanti KnownLdapServers on RemoteIP                     // drop established DCs
| order by FirstSeen desc
let KnownLdapServers = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where DstPortNumber == 389
    | summarize by DstIpAddr;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DstPortNumber in (389, 445)
| summarize Ports = make_set(DstPortNumber), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), ConnCount = count()
        by SrcHostname, DstIpAddr
| where set_has_element(Ports, 389) and set_has_element(Ports, 445)
| join kind=leftanti KnownLdapServers on DstIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| in(field=RemotePort, values=["389","445"])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=[count(as=conns), count(field=RemotePort, distinct=true, as=distinctPorts)])
| distinctPorts>=2
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (389,445) AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="domain_controller" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where mvcount(mvfilter(match(dest_ports,"^389$")))>0 AND mvcount(mvfilter(match(dest_ports,"^445$")))>0
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (389,445) AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="domain_controller" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where mvcount(mvfilter(match(dest_ports,"^389$")))>0 AND mvcount(mvfilter(match(dest_ports,"^445$")))>0
Domain Controller machine account obtains TGT via PKINIT certificate (Certighost impersonation) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the moment the Certighost exploit authenticates as the target DC: a Kerberos AS-REQ (event 4768) for a machine account ($) that uses PKINIT certificate pre-authentication, sourced from a client IP rather than the DC itself. DCs do not normally acquire their own TGTs via issued client certificates, making this a high-signal impersonation indicator. Rationale: Article states the exploit 'uses PKINIT to authenticate as the target Domain Controller.' A 4768 for a $ account carrying Certificate Information fields is exactly that; IpAddress surfaces the attacker workstation for pivoting. Certificate-based TGTs for DC machine accounts are effectively never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.dataminr.com/resources/intel-brief/certighost-cve-2026-54121/
ATT&CKT1649 T1550.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Environments with certificate-based machine authentication where device certs are used for Kerberos (rare)
  • Smartcard/YubiKey pilots misconfigured onto service or machine accounts
  • Third-party PKI onboarding tools testing PKINIT for computer objects
  • AD CS lab/test forests exercising legitimate PKINIT enrollment
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ImpersonatedAccount ($) and SourceIp; confirm the SourceIp is NOT that DC's own address and is not an approved PKINIT device. 2) Contain: if illegitimate, treat the target DC as compromised — rotate krbtgt (twice), revoke the issued certificate on the CA, and isolate the SourceIp host. 3) Hunt: from SourceIp look backward for the CA chase traffic (UC2) and the machine account creation (UC1), and forward for directory replication / DCSync (UC4).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4768
| where TargetUserName endswith "$"   // machine / DC account
| extend CertIssuer = extract(@'CertIssuerName"?>?([^<\r\n]+)', 1, EventData),
         CertSerial = extract(@'CertSerialNumber"?>?([^<\r\n]+)', 1, EventData)
| where isnotempty(CertSerial) and CertSerial !in ("-","")   // PKINIT certificate-based pre-auth
| project TimeGenerated, DC = Computer, ImpersonatedAccount = TargetUserName, SourceIp = IpAddress, CertIssuer, CertSerial
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Directory replication / DCSync of secrets (krbtgt) via impersonated DC identity AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Certighost payoff: using the forged DC credential to request DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All (event 4662), pulling account secrets including krbtgt (a Golden Ticket precursor). Surfaces replication of the directory-changes control-access rights and the source IP requesting them so DC-to-DC baselines can be validated. Rationale: The article's stated impact is DCSync retrieving krbtgt. The DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All GUID (1131f6ad) in 4662 is the canonical DCSync fingerprint; MDI's IdentityDirectoryEvents 'Directory Services replication' additionally yields the source IP, which for Certighost is the attacker host wearing the DC identity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.dataminr.com/resources/intel-brief/certighost-cve-2026-54121/ • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/public-exploit-enables-domain-controller-impersonation • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26
ATT&CKT1003.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate DC-to-DC replication (main source of noise — validate SourceIp against known DC addresses)
  • Entra Connect / AD Connect sync service accounts with replication rights
  • Azure AD Password Hash Sync host performing replication
  • Third-party backup/DR products (e.g. Semperis, Quest) that replicate directory data
  • Security tooling that legitimately holds Get-Changes rights
Suppression filter
| where RequestorAccount !in~ ("MSOL_*","AAD_*","svc-adsync")   // exclude Entra Connect / approved sync accounts; then validate remaining by source IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: on MDI, check SourceIp — if replication was requested from an IP that is NOT a registered DC, AD Connect, or approved sync host, treat as DCSync. 2) Contain: rotate the krbtgt password twice (with the recommended interval), revoke certificates issued by the CA around this window, and isolate SourceIp. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the DC$ PKINIT logon (UC3), the CA chase traffic (UC2), and the low-priv machine account creation (UC1) to reconstruct the full Certighost chain and identify the originating low-privileged account.
IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "Directory Services replication"
| project Timestamp, Requestor = AccountName, RequestorDomain = AccountDomain, TargetDC = DestinationDeviceName, SourceIp = IPAddress, DeviceName, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4662
| where EventData has_any (
    "1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2",   // DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All (secrets incl. krbtgt)
    "1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2",   // DS-Replication-Get-Changes
    "89e95b76-444d-4c62-991a-0facbeda640c")   // DS-Replication-Get-Changes-In-Filtered-Set
| project TimeGenerated, DC = Computer, RequestorAccount = SubjectUserName, RequestorDomain = SubjectDomainName, ObjectName, AccessMask
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Directory Replication Rights Requested (DCSync / krbtgt extraction)

Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54121")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54121")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

CloudAppEvents

| where Result =~ "success"

         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04

logsource:
