ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"

       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

ChatGPT AgentForger Flaw Could Deploy Rogue Workspace Agents via a Phishing Link

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 15 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed a critical vulnerability in OpenAI's ChatGPT Workspace Agents that could have allowed a single phishing link to stealthily build, authorize, and deploy an autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agent inside a victim's organization. The vulnerability has been codenamed AgentForger by Zenity Labs. The issue has since been addressed by OpenAI as of June 8,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ChatGPT AgentForger CSRF link: Agent Builder URL with initial_assistant_prompt param · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AgentForger rogue-agent C2: inbound TASK-subject email followed by outbound reply to sender domain · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ChatGPT AgentForger CSRF link: Agent Builder URL with initial_assistant_prompt param AIDelivery High
Hunts web/Safe-Links clicks and proxy requests to ChatGPT's Agent Builder endpoint (chatgpt.com/agents/studio/new) carrying the initial_assistant_prompt query parameter — the AgentForger CSRF vector that auto-executes an attacker-supplied prompt to stand up a rogue Workspace Agent. Article-specific because the exploit hinges on this exact parameter, which OpenAI removed on 2026-06-08; its presence in traffic is a live exploitation attempt or PoC replay. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit string pair 'chatgpt.com/agents/studio/new' + 'initial_assistant_prompt' from the article and Zenity's primary report; the parameter was patched out on 2026-06-08 so any post-patch sighting is exploitation/PoC. Cross-checked Zenity Labs Part 1, SecurityWeek and The Decoder. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.zenity.io/p/agentforger-part-1-chatgpt-cross-site-agent-forgery • https://www.securityweek.com/openai-fixes-chatgpt-agent-flaw-that-could-let-attackers-forge-an-ai-insider/ • https://the-decoder.com/one-tampered-chatgpt-link-could-spawn-a-rogue-ai-agent-that-took-orders-from-an-attacker-every-five-minutes/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or red team replaying the AgentForger PoC internally
  • Safe Links / CASB URL-detonation sandboxes re-fetching the delivered link
  • DLP or email-security appliances crawling the URL during scanning
  • An analyst pasting the IOC URL into a browser during triage
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the AccountUpn/SrcUsername that received or clicked the link and whether ActionType shows an allowed click; pull the full Url to confirm the embedded initial_assistant_prompt payload. 2) Contain: force-revoke the user's ChatGPT/Workspace session, and in the ChatGPT Enterprise admin console inspect that user's Workspace Agents — delete any agent created from the 'chief-of-staff' template with 'Never ask' connector approvals; rotate connector (Outlook/Gmail/Slack/Teams) tokens. 3) Hunt: search for the same URL delivered to other recipients (EmailUrlInfo), and pivot to the TASK-email C2 detection to see whether a forged agent already began polling for commands.
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Url has "chatgpt.com/agents/studio/new"
| where Url has "initial_assistant_prompt"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Workload, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, IPAddress, Url, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "chatgpt.com/agents/studio/new"
| where Url has "initial_assistant_prompt"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AgentForger rogue-agent C2: inbound TASK-subject email followed by outbound reply to sender domain AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the AgentForger command-and-control loop where the forged Workspace Agent polls the victim mailbox for external emails whose subject begins with 'TASK', executes them, and emails results back to the attacker. Correlates an inbound TASK email from an external domain with an outbound message from the same victim back to that domain within an hour — the agent's request/response C2 signature. Rationale: Uses the article/Zenity-confirmed 'TASK' subject-prefix command convention plus the report-back email loop; the inbound-from-external + outbound-back-to-same-domain correlation raises fidelity above a bare subject match. Cross-checked Zenity Labs Part 1. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.zenity.io/p/agentforger-part-1-chatgpt-cross-site-agent-forgery • https://the-decoder.com/one-tampered-chatgpt-link-could-spawn-a-rogue-ai-agent-that-took-orders-from-an-attacker-every-five-minutes/
ATT&CKT1071.003 T1114.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ticketing/helpdesk workflows where users receive 'TASK' subject emails and reply
  • Project-management or automation tools that email TASK notifications and receive acknowledgements
  • A user genuinely corresponding with an external partner whose threads start with 'TASK'
  • Out-of-office auto-replies bouncing back to an external TASK sender
Suppression filter
| where AttackerDomain !endswith "yourcompany.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the matched Victim mailbox — is the outbound reply machine-generated (rapid, templated, near-identical cadence) and does the AttackerDomain resolve to an unfamiliar external party? Check whether replies recur on a fixed 5-minute offset. 2) Contain: in ChatGPT Enterprise admin, delete any Workspace Agent tied to this user (chief-of-staff template, 'Never ask' connectors), revoke the user's ChatGPT session and mail-connector OAuth tokens, and block the AttackerDomain at the mail gateway. 3) Hunt: enumerate all agents scheduled at repeating short intervals with mail connectors, and pivot back to the AgentForger URL detection to find the original delivery.
let Window = 30d;
let TaskInbound = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Window)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where Subject startswith "TASK"
    | project InTime = Timestamp, Victim = RecipientEmailAddress, AttackerAddr = SenderFromAddress, AttackerDomain = SenderFromDomain;
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Window)
| where EmailDirection == "Outbound"
| extend RecipientDomain = tostring(split(RecipientEmailAddress, "@")[1])
| project OutTime = Timestamp, Victim = SenderFromAddress, ReplyTo = RecipientEmailAddress, RecipientDomain
| join kind=inner TaskInbound on Victim
| where RecipientDomain =~ AttackerDomain
| where OutTime between (InTime .. InTime + 1h)
| project InTime, OutTime, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', OutTime, InTime), Victim, AttackerAddr, ReplyTo, AttackerDomain
| order by OutTime desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access

detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'

    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1486

DeviceFileEvents

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

DeviceEvents

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Hades/VShell C2 beacon to staging infrastructure (IPs, domain, port 21083) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Hermes AI agent running in unattended YOLO mode (auto-approve flag/env) · [LLM] LinPEAS execution and SUID/SGID enumeration sweep for privilege escalation · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Web-server process connecting to internal Hadoop HiveServer2/WebHDFS ports (10000/50070) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a web-tier process (apache/nginx/php-fpm/w3wp) opening a connection to internal Hadoop admin ports 10000 (HiveServer2) or 50070 (WebHDFS), the exact lateral path the operator's hive_rce_py2.py script relied on to reach the ministry's Hadoop cluster. A front-end web server has no legitimate reason to speak the Hive/HDFS wire protocol. Rationale: Anchored on the article's own defensive recommendation ('Alert when a web server process opens a connection to internal Hadoop ports such as 10000 or 50070') and Hunt.io's confirmation that hive_rce_py2.py targeted HiveServer2:10000 plus WebHDFS:50070. Web-tier binary + Hadoop admin port is a high-signal pair rarely seen in normal ops. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/
ATT&CKT1210 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate app server (Superset, Presto client, custom reporting app) co-located on a web host querying HiveServer2
  • Monitoring agents (Prometheus JMX exporter, Ambari agent) polling WebHDFS 50070
  • Data engineers running Beeline from a jump host that also runs a web console
  • PHP-based analytics dashboards designed to read Hive directly
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "superset" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "presto" and DeviceName !has "jump"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host's role — a pure front-end web server has no business speaking Hive/HDFS; inspect the initiating process command line and the user it ran as (www-data/apache = strong signal). 2) Contain: isolate the web host, block egress to the Hadoop subnet on those ports from web-tier hosts, and snapshot the web root for a hidden web shell. 3) Hunt: pull HiveServer2 logs for CREATE FUNCTION ... USING JAR and for java spawning /bin/sh (UC5); check whether HiveServer2 auth is set to NONE.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (10000, 50070)
| where RemoteIPType in ("Private","Reserved")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php","php7.4","php8.1","w3wp.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber in (10000, 50070)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)
| where DvcHostname has_any ("web","www","httpd","nginx","apache") or SrcHostname has_any ("web","www")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hidden dot-prefixed PHP web shell masquerading as a system cache in web root AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of a PHP file whose name begins with a leading dot (hidden from ordinary directory listings) inside a web-served path, matching the operator's web shell planted at /storage/Counter/nine/.journald-cache.php that impersonated a journald cache. Leading-dot PHP in a web root is almost never legitimate. Rationale: Uses the exact TTP Hunt.io flagged: /storage/Counter/nine/.journald-cache.php, a leading-dot PHP file invisible to a normal directory listing and named to imitate a journald cache. The behavioural generalization (leading-dot .php in web root) catches renamed variants while staying near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://securityaffairs.com/195941/hacking/thailands-ministry-of-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent-running-unattended-hades-implant-staged.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Editor swap/backup files like .index.php.swp created by vim (mitigated by requiring .php terminal extension)
  • CMS caching plugins that write dot-prefixed PHP fragments (rare)
  • Developer accidentally committing a .env-style .config.php
  • Composer/vendor tooling writing dot-prefixed helper files into storage/
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vim","vi","nano","composer") and FileName !endswith ".swp"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the file — a leading-dot PHP under a web root is almost always a shell; look for eval/base64_decode/assert/system and check the writing process/user (www-data writing PHP = compromise). 2) Contain: quarantine the file, take the web host offline or block inbound to it, and preserve access logs for requests to that path. 3) Hunt: search all web roots recursively for other leading-dot .php files, correlate first-write time with web-server → Hadoop connections (UC1) and with LinPEAS runs (UC4) on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".php" and FileName startswith "."
| where FolderPath has_any ("/www/","/html/","/htdocs/","/webroot/","/storage/","/var/www")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreated")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php" and TargetFileName startswith "."
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/www/","/html/","/htdocs/","/storage/","/var/www")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hermes AI agent running in unattended YOLO mode (auto-approve flag/env) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a Hermes agent process launched with its auto-approve 'YOLO' setting — the HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1 environment variable or --yolo/​/yolo flag — which disables the human confirmation before each risky command and is the exact configuration the Thai MoF operator used to run post-exploitation unattended. Also surfaces the agent's /hermes-results/ output artifacts. Rationale: The article's central differentiator is the documented YOLO auto-approve mode (--yolo flag, /yolo command, HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1 env var), and Hunt.io confirms the agent wrote to a consistent /hermes-results/ folder. These are unique, near-zero-FP strings that flag an autonomous agent operating without a human in the loop on an internal host. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1651
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sanctioned internal team legitimately running Nous Research Hermes for mail/chore automation in a sandbox
  • Security research or red-team lab intentionally testing Hermes YOLO mode
  • Another unrelated tool that happens to use a --yolo flag (mitigated by requiring the 'hermes' token alongside)
  • Shell history or documentation files containing the literal string being read by a grep/cat
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "lab" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("grep","cat","less","vim")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is not an approved automation sandbox; capture the full command line, parent process, and invoking user, and check for the /hermes-results/ output directory and call_00_*.txt turn logs. 2) Contain: kill the agent process, revoke the account's credentials/keys, and block the host's outbound access pending review (an unattended agent can act fast). 3) Hunt: enumerate what the agent already did — LinPEAS/SUID sweeps (UC4), Hadoop connections (UC1), web-root crawls — and search the network for a HermesWebUI server header or exposed /hermes-results/ directory on port 8878.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--yolo" and ProcessCommandLine has "hermes")
   or ProcessCommandLine has "/hermes-results/"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1"
   or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--yolo" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "hermes")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "/hermes-results/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LinPEAS execution and SUID/SGID enumeration sweep for privilege escalation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation privilege-escalation enumeration the Hermes agent ran on the ministry host: a customized linpeas.sh plus a manual sweep for setuid/setgid binaries (find ... -perm -4000). Pairs the well-known LinPEAS tool with the specific SUID-hunt command the operator used. Rationale: Hunt.io recovered a customized linpeas.sh (checking CVE-2026-31431, CVE-2026-43284/43500, CVE-2026-43503) and the article states the agent ran a 'sweep for elevated-permission binaries' — i.e. a SUID hunt. LinPEAS name + the canonical find -perm -4000 idiom are the two concrete enumeration commands to pivot on. Hunting tier because both appear in sanctioned pentests. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://securityaffairs.com/195941/hacking/thailands-ministry-of-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent-running-unattended-hades-implant-staged.html
ATT&CKT1548.001 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team / pentest engagement running LinPEAS
  • Sysadmins auditing SUID binaries during hardening (CIS benchmark checks often run find -perm -4000)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys agent) enumerating setuid files
  • Backup or compliance scripts that inventory permissions cluster-wide
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("apache2","nginx","php-fpm","sh","bash")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the executing user and parent — LinPEAS run by www-data/apache or a service account (not an admin's interactive shell) is high-signal; correlate with recent web shell writes (UC2) on the same host. 2) Contain: freeze the account, snapshot the host, and check whether any of the four 2026 kernel CVEs' prerequisites (e.g. CAP_NET_ADMIN for Dirty Frag/DirtyClone) hold on that box. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on exploit binaries (mailer.py/CVE-2021-3156, PwnKit/CVE-2021-4034), a Hermes YOLO process (UC3), and outbound C2 (UC6) from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "linpeas")
     or (FileName == "find" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-perm -4000","-perm -u+s","-perm /4000","-perm /u=s"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "linpeas"
     or (TargetProcessName endswith "find" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-perm -4000","-perm -u+s","-perm /4000","-perm /u=s"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HiveServer2 (java) spawning an OS shell — Hive UDF command-execution RCE AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the HiveServer2 Java process spawning a shell or OS command interpreter, the on-host footprint of the operator's HiveCmd.jar user-defined function that turns ordinary Hive queries into arbitrary command execution as the Hive service account. A database engine forking /bin/sh is a classic UDF-abuse RCE signal. Rationale: Hunt.io confirms hive_rce_py2.py installed HiveCmd.jar as a Hive UDF to run OS commands through SQL queries as the Hive service account. The victim-side artifact is HiveServer2/java forking a shell — a direct, high-fidelity RCE signal that also generalizes past this specific jar. Datadog leg pivots on the recovered filenames since auditd lacks reliable parent-process linkage. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hive transform/TRANSFORM queries that legitimately invoke shell scripts or python streaming
  • Hadoop admin jobs where java (YARN/MapReduce) spawns helper shells during normal ETL
  • Monitoring or health-check scripts wrapping hive/beeline that shell out
  • Custom sanctioned Hive UDFs that call external binaries
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "TRANSFORM" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "yarn" and ProcessCommandLine !has "healthcheck"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and the HiveServer2 query/session that triggered it; pull HiveServer2 logs for CREATE TEMPORARY FUNCTION ... USING JAR and for a jar named HiveCmd.jar or added via ADD JAR. 2) Contain: kill the child process, remove the malicious UDF/jar, rotate the Hive service-account credentials, and set HiveServer2 authentication away from NONE while restricting who can register UDFs. 3) Hunt: trace the source of the Hive connection (UC1 web-server → 10000), check for the staged hive_full_v3.tar.gz / ambari_cmd.json tooling, and review other cluster nodes for the same jar.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("HiveServer2","org.apache.hive","HiveCmd.jar") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java","hive")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","curl","wget","chmod","nc","ncat","python","python2","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("HiveServer2","org.apache.hive","HiveCmd.jar") or ActingProcessName endswith "java"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","curl","wget","chmod","nc","ncat","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hades/VShell C2 beacon to staging infrastructure (IPs, domain, port 21083) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host callbacks to the operator's confirmed command-and-control and staging infrastructure: four Hong Kong/Malaysia IPs, the redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com domain, and the VShell listener on TCP 21083. Also anchors on the Hades Go implant and VShell stage payload hashes for host-side confirmation. Rationale: Hunt.io's IOC table (second source beyond The Hacker News, also reported by BleepingComputer/SecurityAffairs) lists these four IPs, the redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com domain, VShell on TCP 21083, and SHA-256 hashes for the Hades Linux/Windows implants and VShell stages. Direct-IOC alerting on confirmed C2 infrastructure is high-confidence and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195941/hacking/thailands-ministry-of-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent-running-unattended-hades-implant-staged.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or research infrastructure scanning/sinkholing the same IPs (benign, but investigate)
  • Shared hosting: one of the Hong Kong ASNs later reassigned to a legitimate service on the same IP
  • Security tooling (VirusTotal retro-hunt, honeypot) deliberately connecting to the IOC
  • An analyst's sandbox detonating the sample and beaconing out
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vt-scanner","nmap","masscan") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a masquerading name (kworker, multipathd, accounts-daemon, dwm_33b7.exe, ctfmon) beaconing to these IPs is Hades/VShell; hash the binary and compare to the published SHA-256s (e.g. d252ee7b34…c7d1e2 Hades Linux, 0f8c905a…85f2fc VShell Linux stage 1). 2) Contain: block the four IPs, port 21083, and sinkhole redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com; isolate the beaconing host and kill the implant. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the implant hashes and the Hades HTTP beacon URIs (/assets/app.min.js, /assets/vendor.js, /assets/main.js with UA 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36'), and review how the implant was staged (web shell UC2 / Hive RCE UC5).
let c2ips = dynamic(["43.246.208.207","103.97.0.57","118.107.222.232","202.181.27.115"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2ips) or RemoteUrl has "redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com" or RemotePort == 21083
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2ips = dynamic(["43.246.208.207","103.97.0.57","118.107.222.232","202.181.27.115"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImNetworkSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DstIpAddr in (c2ips) or DstPortNumber == 21083
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Dvc=DvcHostname),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery has "redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname=SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DnsQuery)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

            - '\mshta.exe'

let BadHashes = dynamic(["0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f"]);

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 18 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The threat actors behind the Golden Chickens malware-as-a-service (MaaS) ecosystem have resurfaced with four new malware families, indicating that the operators are showing no signs of stopping despite extensive public disclosures into their inner workings. The malware families in question are: TinyEgg, ChonkyChicken, a modularized variant of ChonkyChicken, and a modified web browser credential

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Golden Chickens TinyEgg/ChonkyChicken OCX side-load via regsvr32 from user-writable paths · [LLM] TAG-195 WinComCtl Run-key persistence pointing to staged OCX · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Golden Chickens WebSocket C2 from regsvr32/rundll32 to non-standard port 3000 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ChonkyChicken browser session hijack via Chrome/Edge remote-debugging (CDP) off-screen · [LLM] ChromEggscalator ABE-bypass debug log and OCX staging artifacts · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Golden Chickens TinyEgg/ChonkyChicken OCX side-load via regsvr32 from user-writable paths AIInstallation High
Hunts regsvr32.exe registering an .ocx payload from %TEMP%/%LOCALAPPDATA%/Downloads/Packages, which is TAG-195's shared delivery model for TinyEgg, ChonkyChicken and ChromEggscalator (updater.ocx, mscomctl.ocx, chromelevator.ocx, mscom.ocx via /i, DllInstall or DllRegisterServer). Article-specific because it pins the LOLBin+extension+location+filename set the campaign reuses across all four families. Rationale: Anchored on RF's finding that all four families are packaged as OCX and launched with regsvr32 + filename-gating on updater.ocx/mscomctl.ocx/chromelevator.ocx/mscom.ocx from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages and %TEMP%; regsvr32 registering an .ocx from a user profile is near-zero in benign fleets. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://cybersecuritynews.com/chonkychicken-steals-chrome-credentials/ • https://gbhackers.com/four-modular-malware-families/
ATT&CKT1218.010 T1218.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ActiveX/OCX installers run from a user Downloads folder during app deployment
  • Developer or QA registering a self-built .ocx from a build output dir under AppData
  • Software packaging tools (SCCM/Intune) staging OCX controls in Temp before registration
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that ship mscomctl.ocx and self-register on first run
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full regsvr32 command line and parent process; confirm the OCX path is user-writable and hash the .ocx (VT/RF lookup). Check for the WinComCtl Run key on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the regsvr32 process tree, quarantine the .ocx, and block the staging domain/IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same OCX filenames, for Chrome/Edge launched with --remote-debugging-port, and for outbound WebSocket to port 3000.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "regsvr32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".ocx"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("updater.ocx","mscomctl.ocx","chromelevator.ocx","mscom.ocx")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Packages\") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/i","/s","DllInstall","DllRegisterServer"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\regsvr32.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".ocx"
| where CommandLine has_any ("updater.ocx","mscomctl.ocx","chromelevator.ocx","mscom.ocx")
   or (CommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Packages\") and CommandLine has_any ("/i","/s","DllInstall","DllRegisterServer"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

TAG-195 WinComCtl Run-key persistence pointing to staged OCX AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the HKCU ...\CurrentVersion\Run value named WinComCtl (or any Run value pointing to a regsvr32-invoked .ocx under Packages/AppData), the shared persistence approach across TinyEgg and ChonkyChicken. Registry pivot distinct from the process-creation UC. Rationale: RF documents the exact value name (WinComCtl) under HKCU Run pointing at the staged OCX in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages; the value-name string plus .ocx autostart data is a high-fidelity, campaign-unique persistence artifact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://cyberpress.org/golden-chickens-unleashes-tinyegg/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche app legitimately auto-starting a registered OCX control via a Run value
  • IT deployment scripts writing Run keys that call regsvr32 for a required control
  • Software using the generic value name 'WinComCtl' for a real Common Controls dependency (rare)
  • Backup/restore tooling recreating a previously-existing Run value
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryValueData has @"\Program Files\" or RegistryValueData has @"\Windows\System32\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump RegistryValueData to get the exact OCX path + regsvr32 args; correlate with the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) and check whether that OCX exists on disk. 2) Contain: isolate host, delete the Run value, quarantine the referenced OCX, and capture it for analysis before deletion. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing process across the fleet and look for regsvr32-OCX executions and port-3000 WebSocket C2 from the same hosts.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "WinComCtl"
   or (RegistryValueData has ".ocx" and RegistryValueData has_any ("regsvr32", @"\Packages\", @"\AppData\Local\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "WinComCtl"
   or (RegistryValueData has ".ocx" and RegistryValueData has_any ("regsvr32", @"\Packages\", @"\AppData\Local\"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
title: TAG-195 WinComCtl Run Key Persistence to OCX

ChonkyChicken browser session hijack via Chrome/Edge remote-debugging (CDP) off-screen AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Chrome/Edge/Brave launched with --remote-debugging-port and the tell-tale off-screen --window-position=-32000,-32000 (and/or a non-browser parent supplying --user-data-dir), which is how ChonkyChicken drives live browser sessions over Chrome DevTools Protocol for credential and session theft. Distinct process-tree pivot. Rationale: RF details ChonkyChicken launching Chrome/Edge with --remote-debugging-port=9222, --user-data-dir and --window-position=-32000,-32000 driving a local 127.0.0.1:9222 CDP endpoint; the off-screen window flag plus remote-debugging is a textbook covert-CDP signal with negligible benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://cybersecuritynews.com/chonkychicken-steals-chrome-credentials/ • https://www.cryptika.com/chonkychicken-malware-steals-chrome-credentials-moves-laterally-and-spies-on-victims/
ATT&CKT1185 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated browser test frameworks (Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright) launching Chrome with --remote-debugging-port on QA hosts
  • RPA bots driving a headless browser for legitimate automation
  • Developers debugging web apps with remote debugging enabled
  • Kiosk/monitoring software that positions a browser off-screen
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","chromedriver.exe","pwsh.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\", @"\selenium\", @"\ci\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process of the browser launch — a non-browser parent (regsvr32/rundll32/unknown) with --remote-debugging-port is high-confidence malicious; confirm no CI/RPA tooling on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, terminate the browser + parent tree, and force-reset the user's browser-backed credentials and session tokens. 3) Hunt: check the same host for regsvr32-OCX execution, WinComCtl Run key, xlog.txt in ProgramData, and port-3000 WebSocket C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--window-position=-32000"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--user-data-dir" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\brave.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where CommandLine has "--window-position=-32000"
   or (CommandLine has "--user-data-dir" and not(ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe")))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Browser Launched with Remote Debugging Off-Screen (ChonkyChicken CDP Hijack)

Golden Chickens WebSocket C2 from regsvr32/rundll32 to non-standard port 3000 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections initiated by regsvr32.exe/rundll32.exe (the processes hosting the OCX implants) to public IPs on the non-standard WebSocket C2 port 3000, plus the campaign's known C2 IPs/domains. A LOLBin making an internet WebSocket connection is the TinyEgg/ChonkyChicken beacon shape. Rationale: RF reports the WebSocket C2 uses non-standard port 3000 with endpoint /ws/agent and lists C2 IPs (65.20.102.161/105.177, 108.61.209.100) and domains (xtrafftrck.net, thessa.trackgrid.net); pairing that with the OCX-host process (regsvr32/rundll32) reaching a public IP is near-zero benign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://gbhackers.com/four-modular-malware-families/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal dev service listening on port 3000 (Node.js default) reached by a legitimately signed tool — but rarely by regsvr32
  • Rundll32 hosting a legitimate control that phones a vendor endpoint on a high port
  • Proxy/PAC rewrites that make regsvr32 traffic appear to hit an unexpected port
  • Security tooling that proxies EDR telemetry over 3000
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIPType == "Private")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating regsvr32/rundll32 command line references an .ocx and resolve the remote IP/domain reputation (RF/VT). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the C2 IPs/domains and port 3000 egress at the perimeter, and kill the OCX host process. 3) Hunt: reverse the join — find all hosts talking to the same C2 IPs, then check each for the WinComCtl Run key and OCX side-loads.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort == 3000
   or RemoteIP in ("65.20.102.161","65.20.105.177","108.61.209.100","70.34.205.43")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("xtrafftrck.net","trackgrid.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
| where DstPortNumber == 3000
   or DstIpAddr in ("65.20.102.161","65.20.105.177","108.61.209.100","70.34.205.43")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
