Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620") or SHA1 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620") or MD5 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620") or SHA1 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620") or MD5 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Attackers Weaponize GitHub Actions Runners to Target cPanel and WHM Servers

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 17 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have shed light on a large-scale campaign that has turned compromised GitHub repositories into distributed attack infrastructure designed to target cPanel and WebHost Manager (WHM) instances. The activity involves malicious Packagist development versions spanning 10 packages associated with a legitimate PHP and DevOps developer, dinushchathurya, between July 12 and 13,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Inbound scanning of cPanel/WHM control-panel ports (CVE-2026-41940 exploitation) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network callback to GitHub Actions cPanel-campaign C2 43.228.157.68 · [LLM] DNSHook beacon to dnshook.site (campaign UUID f5b0b742-...) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Network callback to GitHub Actions cPanel-campaign C2 43.228.157.68 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host in the estate (self-hosted runner, web/hosting server, or workstation) that connects to the campaign's command-and-control server at 43.228.157.68, which serves the architecture-specific Linux scanning/exploitation payload and receives HTTP POST uploads of harvested AWS/GitHub/Stripe/SSH secrets. This is the single hard network IOC from the campaign. Rationale: 43.228.157.68 is the explicit C2 IP named in the article and confirmed by Socket's writeup as the host serving architecture-matched Linux payloads and receiving credential POST uploads; a single-IP match on a known-bad indicator is inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/attackers-weaponize-github-actions.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or red-team validation traffic deliberately probing the published IOC
  • A sinkhole/DNS-blocklist appliance that proxies blocked destinations to a decoy
  • Vulnerability scanner configured with the IOC as a test target
  • Shared-NAT egress where an unrelated tenant reached the IP before takedown
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and account on the connecting host; determine whether it is a CI/CD runner, hosting server, or user endpoint, and whether the process matches a downloaded/renamed Linux binary. 2) Contain: block 43.228.157.68 at egress firewall/proxy, isolate the host, and rotate every secret class the campaign targets (AWS keys, GitHub/GitLab tokens, Stripe/SendGrid/Mailgun, SSH keys, DB creds) reachable from that host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for outbound POSTs to dnshook.site and for inbound connections to cPanel/WHM ports 2082/2083/2086/2087.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "43.228.157.68"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "43.228.157.68" or SourceIP == "43.228.157.68"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNSHook beacon to dnshook.site (campaign UUID f5b0b742-...) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution of *.dnshook.site, the DNS-based exfiltration/telemetry channel the campaign embeds in ~6,100 malicious GitHub Actions workflow files carrying the unique DNSHook identifier f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d. Any internal host resolving this domain indicates a runner or server executing the weaponized workflow payload. Rationale: dnshook.site plus the unique DNSHook GUID f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d are article-specific IOCs tied by Socket to ~6,100 workflow files across the broader campaign; a DNS suffix match on this domain is high-fidelity and catches variant subdomains. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/attackers-weaponize-github-actions.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating a sample that resolves the domain
  • DNS firewall passive-DNS logging that pre-resolves blocklist entries
  • An internal threat-intel enrichment job querying the IOC domain
  • Typosquat coincidence where an unrelated legitimate service shares the dnshook string (verify full label)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying ClientIP/host and the process that triggered the lookup; confirm whether it hosts or checked out any dinushchathurya Packagist package or GitHub workflow. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block *.dnshook.site at the resolver, isolate the host, and revoke tokens/keys accessible from it. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host's outbound connections to 43.228.157.68 and inbound activity on cPanel/WHM ports, and sweep the repo/CI estate for workflow files containing the GUID f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteUrl has "dnshook.site" or RemoteUrl has "f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "dnshook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, ResultCode, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound scanning of cPanel/WHM control-panel ports (CVE-2026-41940 exploitation) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound connections to cPanel (2082/2083) and WHM (2086/2087) control-panel ports, the surface the campaign's Linux payload scans and attacks via the CVE-2026-41940 authentication bypass before harvesting configuration files, DB access, SSH material, and cloud keys. Flags volumetric probing and any activity sourced from the campaign C2 43.228.157.68. Rationale: cPanel/WHM listen on the well-known ports 2082/2083/2086/2087 that CVE-2026-41940 (the article's named auth-bypass CVE) is exploited against; pairing the port set with inbound direction plus the known C2 source IP keeps the volumetric hunt article-specific rather than generic port-scan noise. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/attackers-weaponize-github-actions.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate reseller/hosting admins logging into WHM (2087) and cPanel (2083) from mobile/rotating ISP IPs
  • Uptime/monitoring tools polling 2083/2087 health endpoints at high frequency
  • Load-balancer or reverse-proxy health checks against control-panel ports
  • Authorized migration tooling (e.g. WHM transfer) enumerating multiple accounts
  • Internal vulnerability scanner sweeping the hosting subnet
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: exclude known admin/monitoring egress before thresholding
| where SourceIP !in ("<none>") // replace with allow-list watchlist join: | join kind=leftanti (_GetWatchlist('HostingAdminIPs')) on $left.SourceIP == $right.IPAddress
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank source IPs by target-host count and port spread; confirm whether the top sources are known admin/monitoring IPs or the C2 43.228.157.68 / cloud-runner ASNs. 2) Contain: block unrecognized scanning sources at the perimeter, confirm cPanel/WHM is patched against CVE-2026-41940, and force-rotate any panel and API credentials on hosts that received connections. 3) Hunt: on any host that answered a probe, check for outbound to 43.228.157.68 and dnshook.site, review /usr/local/cpanel logs for auth-bypass sessions, and audit for newly exfiltrated SSH keys, DB creds, and cloud keys.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort

| order by conn_count desc

| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-41940")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-41940")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

SecurityEvent

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

CloudAppEvents

          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:

      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel

Cisco Talos
2026-07-23 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chaos ransomware group uses new malware "msaRAT" that hijacks browsers. The malware doesn't communicate directly with C2 but connects through the browser. It enables arbitrary command execution while hiding the attacker's IP from victims via WebRTC over TURN.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] msaRAT delivery: curl.exe fetching fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData over HTTP
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] msaRAT msiexec executing update_ms.msi (fake Windows update custom action)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] msaRAT CDP abuse: headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging port spawned by non-browser parent · [LLM] msaRAT C2 network IOC: connection to 172.86.126.18 or is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
msaRAT delivery: curl.exe fetching fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData over HTTP AIDelivery High
Hunts the Chaos ransomware pre-ransom delivery step where curl.exe downloads update_ms.msi from attacker IP 172.86.126.18 (plain HTTP on port 443) into C:\programdata\. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact filename, ProgramData sink, and hardcoded C2 IP. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim curl command from the article (update_ms.msi, hardcoded 172.86.126.18, ProgramData sink) — the triple combination is essentially unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199 • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/new-chaos-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using curl to stage a genuine .msi in ProgramData for software deployment
  • Internal software-distribution tooling pulling installers over HTTP to a ProgramData staging folder
  • Security researcher / detection-lab replaying the sample
  • RMM agent using curl to fetch an update package into ProgramData
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible.exe","chocolatey.exe","choco.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "172.86.126.18")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the curl invocation targeted 172.86.126.18 or the literal update_ms.msi filename and that the destination is C:\programdata\; pull the parent process and user. 2. Contain: network-isolate the host, block 172.86.126.18 at the perimeter, and quarantine C:\programdata\update_ms.msi before it is executed by msiexec. 3. Hunt: pivot to msiexec execution of that MSI, headless Chrome/Edge launches with --remote-debugging-port, and outbound traffic to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update_ms.msi", "172.86.126.18")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "programdata"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "curl.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("update_ms.msi", "172.86.126.18")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "programdata"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT msiexec executing update_ms.msi (fake Windows update custom action) AIInstallation High
Hunts the second delivery stage: msiexec.exe executing the Chaos-dropped update_ms.msi whose custom action CA_Run_EA2AEBC3 reflectively loads lib.dll (msaRAT) into memory. Article-specific via the exact MSI filename. Rationale: The MSI filename update_ms.msi is a verbatim article IOC; msiexec running it from ProgramData is the reflective-load launcher for lib.dll (msaRAT). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor MSI happening to be staged in ProgramData (broad hunting clause only)
  • Patch-management tool invoking msiexec against a ProgramData-cached installer
  • Detection-lab replay of the sample
  • Third-party updater masquerading its own installer in ProgramData
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm msiexec ran update_ms.msi and inspect the MSI's Binary table / custom action (CA_Run_*) and file metadata spoofing Microsoft. 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill any child processes, and capture memory before reboot to recover the in-memory lib.dll (msaRAT). 3. Hunt: look for the RUN export being invoked, headless browser launches with CDP flags, and workers.dev / Twilio TURN egress to confirm C2 establishment.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where TargetProcessName has "msiexec.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\programdata\" and TargetProcessCommandLine has ".msi")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT CDP abuse: headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging port spawned by non-browser parent AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts msaRAT's core 'living off the browser' behaviour — it launches Chrome or Edge in headless mode with the CDP remote-debugging port enabled to drive a covert WebRTC C2. Detects browsers started with --headless/--remote-debugging-port by a parent that is not a browser or explorer. Rationale: The article states msaRAT launches Chrome/Edge headless via CreateProcessW with the remote-debugging port enabled to drive CDP; a browser started with these flags by a non-browser parent is a high-fidelity signal of programmatic browser hijack. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chaes-malware-now-uses-google-chrome-devtools-protocol-to-steal-data/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium automation frameworks launching headless Chrome for testing
  • CI/CD build agents rendering pages via headless Chrome
  • PDF-generation or web-scraping services spawning headless browsers
  • Developer tooling that opens Chrome with --remote-debugging-port for debugging
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe", "python.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cypress.exe", "chromedriver.exe", "selenium.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the parent process that spawned the headless browser and the remote-debugging port; benign automation parents (node.exe from a known project) differ sharply from msiexec/rundll32/unknown. 2. Contain: if the parent is unexpected, isolate the host and terminate the browser + parent process tree, then capture memory for the in-memory msaRAT. 3. Hunt: correlate with the CDP JSON endpoint (/json/list/) on localhost, WebRTC/TURN egress to global.turn.twilio.com, and connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port", "--headless")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "msedgewebview2.exe", "userinit.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port", "--headless")
| where not(ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "msedgewebview2.exe", "userinit.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT C2 network IOC: connection to 172.86.126.18 or is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network contact with the hardcoded Chaos/msaRAT infrastructure — the delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the Cloudflare Workers signaling endpoint is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev used for SDP/ICE exchange. Pure IOC pivot corroborated by Talos. Rationale: Both the delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the Cloudflare Workers signaling domain are verbatim, campaign-unique IOCs from the Talos article; direct network matches are the highest-fidelity possible pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate host also using an unrelated *.workers.dev service (mitigated by the exact subdomain match)
  • Threat-intel sandbox / detonation VM deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Security scanner probing the attacker IP
  • Proxy log replay from an IR investigation
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the source host and the initiating process (a browser process for the workers.dev signaling, or curl/msiexec for the delivery IP). 2. Contain: block 172.86.126.18 and is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev at the firewall/proxy and network-isolate the source host. 3. Hunt: on the host, look back for the curl download of update_ms.msi, msiexec execution, headless browser launch with CDP flags, RMM tooling, and outbound Twilio TURN (global.turn.twilio.com) traffic indicating the WebRTC DataChannel is live.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18" or RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "172.86.126.18" or DestinationHostName =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or RequestURL has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |

    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Nine-Year-Old RefluXFS Linux Flaw Gives Local Users Root on Default RHEL Installs

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 15 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

RefluXFS, a Linux kernel flaw disclosed on July 22 and tracked as CVE-2026-64600, lets an unprivileged local user overwrite root-owned files on an XFS filesystem and gain persistent root access. Qualys said default installations of Red Hat Enterprise Linux and its derivatives, Fedora Server, and Amazon Linux can meet the conditions for exploitation. The company demonstrated the race against

Exposure hunt: unpatched CVE-2026-64600 (RefluXFS) on reflink-XFS RHEL/Fedora/Amazon Linux AIExploitation High
Surfaces Linux hosts still exposed to the RefluXFS XFS reflink race (CVE-2026-64600) that grants local users root. Because the exploit leaves no runtime log trace, patch-state inventory is the primary control — this hunts every device where TVM still reports the CVE unremediated. Rationale: Anchored on the exact CVE id CVE-2026-64600 from the article; the piece stresses that reflink-enabled XFS RHEL/Fedora/Amazon Linux default installs are exposed and that no behavioural artifact is produced, so TVM patch-state is the highest-fidelity signal available. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/07/22/14 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/linux/new-refluxfs-linux-flaw-lets-attackers-gain-root-privileges/
ATT&CKT1068
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host patched but has not re-checked in — kernel installed on disk yet the running kernel is still vulnerable (article warns installing the package doesn't replace the in-memory kernel until reboot), so a rebooted-but-not-rescanned host can look exposed
  • RHEL 7 XFS volumes flagged despite predating reflink support (not actually exploitable)
  • Air-gapped/offline hosts with stale TVM inventory
  • Devices where XFS reflink is not enabled (reflink=0) but TVM still maps the CVE to the kernel package
  • Short-lived CI/build VMs that appear and vanish before remediation
Suppression filter
| where VulnerabilitySeverityLevel in ("High","Critical")
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host run `xfs_info / | grep reflink=` (and on any other mounted XFS volume) to confirm reflink=1 — only reflink-enabled volumes are exploitable; confirm the RUNNING kernel via `uname -r` against the fixed RHSA build, not just the installed package. 2) Contain: prioritise multi-tenant / shared-shell / CI hosts where untrusted local code runs; apply the vendor errata (RHSA-2026:39179/39180 for RHEL 8, RHSA-2026:39494 for RHEL 10) and REBOOT to load the fixed kernel. 3) Hunt: on any host that was exposed while untrusted users had shell access, pivot to the chsh-precondition and passwordless-root UCs below to check for actual exploitation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-64600"
| where OSPlatform == "Linux"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-64600"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
RefluXFS precondition reset: unprivileged chsh execution enabling the reflink race AIExploitation Low
The RefluXFS race only fires when the target block starts unshared; the Qualys advisory states an unprivileged user can reset that condition by running chsh. This hunts non-root invocations of chsh, which in isolation is benign but is an article-specific setup step for the exploit. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit statement that 'an unprivileged user can reset that condition by running chsh' — a concrete, article-specific setup action for CVE-2026-64600, though intentionally low-confidence/high-FP since chsh is a legitimate shell-change tool. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/07/22/14
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user changing their own login shell (e.g. bash to zsh) via chsh
  • Provisioning/config-management tooling (Ansible, cloud-init) setting user shells at build time
  • Developer onboarding scripts standardising shells
  • Interactive troubleshooting by a user who genuinely wants a different shell
  • Container image build steps invoking chsh
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","python3","cloud-init","useradd","adduser")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the same host+user also appears in the CVE-2026-64600 exposure hunt (reflink-XFS, unpatched running kernel) — chsh on a non-vulnerable or patched host is almost certainly benign. 2) Contain: if the host is confirmed exposed and the user is untrusted (CI runner, shared shell), snapshot the host and restrict that account's local execution pending review. 3) Hunt: correlate this chsh event with any root shell / su-to-root by the same user within the following minutes (see passwordless-root UC) and inspect /etc/passwd and setuid-root binaries for content that no longer matches the package baseline (rpm -Va).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName == "chsh"
| where AccountName !in~ ("root","system") and AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "chsh"
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("root","system")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RefluXFS post-exploit: passwordless root session shortly after unprivileged chsh AIExploitation Medium
The RefluXFS demo strips the root password in /etc/passwd via a block-layer write that bypasses the inode, leaving no file-event trace. This alerts when a non-root user runs the chsh precondition step and then obtains a root shell (su/sudo/root shell) on the same host within a short window — the observable outcome of the escalation. Rationale: Ties two concrete article behaviours — the chsh precondition reset and the demo's outcome of a passwordless root shell after /etc/passwd is overwritten at the block layer — into a temporal correlation, which is stronger than either signal alone given the exploit produces no file/kernel logs. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/linux/new-refluxfs-linux-flaw-lets-attackers-gain-root-privileges/
ATT&CKT1068 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin legitimately changing their shell with chsh and then using sudo/su for normal admin work in the same session
  • Automation account that both adjusts shells and elevates for maintenance within a 10-minute window
  • Shared jump host where multiple users' chsh and su activity coincidentally overlap on the same DeviceId
  • Break-glass/root-console maintenance windows
  • Configuration-management run that sets a shell then executes privileged tasks
Suppression filter
| where DelaySec <= 120
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is exposed to CVE-2026-64600 (reflink-XFS, vulnerable running kernel) and inspect how root was obtained — run `rpm -Va` / compare /etc/passwd and setuid-root binaries against package baselines, since a block-layer overwrite leaves mtime/perms/setuid bit intact but changes content. 2) Contain: isolate the host, invalidate the root credential/root session, and force a reboot onto a patched kernel; preserve a disk image (on-disk block change is the only forensic artifact). 3) Hunt: from the compromised host pivot to root-context reads of /etc/shadow and SSH keys, and outbound SSH/recon from its IP to find lateral movement following the escalation.
let Window = 10m;
let Precondition = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName == "chsh"
    | where AccountName !in~ ("root","system") and AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project ChshTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, EscalatingUser = AccountName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("su","sudo") or (FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh") and AccountName =~ "root")
| join kind=inner Precondition on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ChshTime .. ChshTime + Window)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, EscalatingUser, RootProcess = FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChshTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ChshTime)
| order by Timestamp desc
let Window = 10m;
let Precondition = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetProcessName has "chsh"
    | where ActorUsername !in~ ("root","system")
    | project ChshTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EscalatingUser = ActorUsername;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("su","sudo") or (TargetProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh") and TargetUsername =~ "root")
| join kind=inner Precondition on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ChshTime .. ChshTime + Window)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EscalatingUser, RootProcess = TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ChshTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ChshTime)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/chsh$/i UserName!=root
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(su|sudo)$/i}, field=aid, include=[ComputerName, CommandLine, ImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count())

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'

    selection_child:

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
